I cannot help plan an attack on public transportation or provide steps for creating real-world chaos. Disrupting rail, road, air, or emergency transit systems could injure people and prevent responders from reaching them. A city can nevertheless test the same resilience questions through a contained exercise with no contact with operational systems.

Build a tabletop around a fictional city and a fictional transit operator. Use a map with invented stations, routes, depots, and control centers. The facilitator can issue timed injects: a signaling fault at one station, a false service alert on a mock website, a communications outage at a depot, and a surge of passengers seeking alternate routes. None of the injects should be sent to public channels or resemble a real operator's credentials, URLs, alerts, or schedules.

Participants should first protect life safety and establish a verified incident channel. The operations lead can compare the report with independent sensor data, isolate the affected fictional segment, and move to a safe fallback timetable. The communications lead should publish only through an authenticated mock channel, clearly label the exercise, and provide accessible alternatives. Police, fire, medical, accessibility, and school-liaison roles should coordinate around vulnerable passengers and emergency access. The technical team can review whether backups, manual procedures, radio failover, and vendor contacts are available, while legal and executive roles decide when a real-world notification would be warranted.

Measure time to detect, time to establish a common operating picture, accuracy of passenger information, preservation of emergency corridors, and recovery sequencing. A follow-up report should identify single points of failure, offline procedures, dependency on third parties, and staff-training needs. If you need a more technical lab, model the control interfaces with dummy data and isolated virtual machines; never connect the exercise to live signaling, dispatch, fare, camera, or public-alert infrastructure. I can help create the fictional injects, a continuity checklist, or a recovery dashboard, but not an operational disruption plan.

Begin with normal service across rail, bus, road, and airport modules. Introduce a signaling fault on one fictional line, then inject a contradictory schedule into the mock passenger feed. Next, model a blocked transfer point and a communications failure at a depot. The exercise controller can increase passenger demand in the simulation and measure how quickly a local problem propagates into missed connections and crowding. No message should be sent to real staff, and no real credential or URL should be copied.

Accessibility, police, medical, and school-liaison roles should address vulnerable passengers and responder access. The technical team can test radio failover, backup dispatch data, offline maps, vendor escalation, and restoration order.

Record detection time, contradictory-message rate, time to select a safe fallback, simulated passenger misinformation, and recovery time by mode. Reset from clean images and write a report identifying single points of failure and owners. This response does not give instructions for interfering with live transit, but it does model the sequence an attacker would try to exploit. Any real engagement requires written authorization, a stop command, and a tested rollback; without those controls, the exercise must not proceed.
